visual.general_description: Three-panel color photograph series (A-C) illustrating the wound-treatment method: an open abdominal wound, the same type of wound covered by green mesh, and a foam dressing with suction pad and tubing.
visual.detailed_description: Panels A and B are top-down views of an open elongated abdominal wound, first showing pale fibrinous material with stitches in the bed and then the bed covered by a green-teal mesh. Panel C is a close-up of a dark grey foam strip with round suction pad and clear tubing beside an adhesive patch. Panels are labeled A, B, C in white boxes at the upper left. No other text, scale or arrows are visible. Panel A looks similar to Fig. 2A, but this resemblance was not used for attribution.

panels.general_description: Color photograph of an open, elongated abdominal wound with red margins and pale fibrinous material in the central bed.
panels.detailed_description: Top-down color photograph of a vertically elongated open skin wound on the abdomen. The wound edges are red and the central bed holds pale white-yellow fibrous or necrotic-looking material with several dark blue suture or stitch segments scattered along its length. Red granulating-looking tissue lines both lateral margins and the lower end. A small round skin indentation (umbilicus-like) lies at the lower right outside the wound edge. Surrounding skin is pale tan with scattered fine hair. No scale, label, arrow or text is visible.

evidence.quote:
Fig. 1
Method for using Sorbact in combination with NPWTi-d. (A) The necrotic tissue is debrided and irrigated at the wound margin or wound bed. (B) Sorbact is placed on the wound bed to absorb bacteria and prevent adhesion between the foam and tissue. (C) The foam is packed, and negative pressure is initiated at 125 mmHg. In cases with exposed intestines, pressure is started at 50 mmHg with caution to avoid perforation, and is gradually increased according to granulation tissue formation.NPWTi-d, negative pressure wound therapy with instillation and dwell time
